piezas.titulo: Meta Welcomes Loblaw as First Canadian Retail Partner to Muse
piezas.cuerpo: Starting today, Loblaw is bringing its catalogue to Muse as a partner connector, the first Canadian retailer to do so. Connectors are a big reason Muse can do so much. Canadians can connect their Muse to apps they already use, including Gmail, Google Calendar and Instagram, so it can help them manage email, coordinate schedules and draw on saved content to get everyday tasks done. With participating Loblaw banners, Canadian shoppers can now ask Muse to help with meal planning, build their basket and check-out, all in Muse. Muse can remember brand preferences and information like food allergies, making next week’s planning even easier. Making this technology work for everyone requires careful design and engineering to operate more safely. Muse runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated computer in the cloud that securely stores the data and credentials for the services you connect, while keeping passwords and payment methods out of the agent’s view. You choose what your Muse can access, and it checks with you before sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase. piezas.titulo: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
piezas.cuerpo: Scientists and fishers study how these ‘reefs’ and the creatures living on them are transforming the ocean floor – and what it means for the fishing industry A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel. DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’” Continue reading...
